en: The Scripture on Māra’s Trial of Maudgalyāyana, also known as the Scripture on Māra’s Disturbance, translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi people during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Vṛji, staying at Mount Puṣpavanta in the village of Bhayaṃkara.
In the garden.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was walking in meditation during the darkness of night, pacing back and forth along a level path.
Then, the Wicked Māra went to where the Buddha was and, by his own supernatural power, transformed himself into a shadow that entered into Maudgalyāyana’s belly.
The venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:
"Why does my belly rumble like thunder?
It is as if a hungry man were carrying a heavy burden."
"I shall enter my room and attain the Samādhi of Right Reception to observe its source.

Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana immediately entered his room and, through samādhi, observed his own body; he instantly beheld the Wicked Māra manifesting a phantom that had penetrated into his belly, and he said to him:
"Wicked Māra!"
"Go forth! Go forth!
Do not disturb the Tathāgata and his disciples, lest you suffer for a long night in unrest and fall into the evil realms.
The Māra thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa has never before seen me, nor does he know me, yet he recklessly utters false words:
'Evil Māra! Get out, get out! "
"Do not harass the Tathāgata and his disciples, lest you incur suffering and unrest for a long night.
Even though my teacher, the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, does not yet know me, how much less so his disciples?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "I further know what you are currently thinking in your heart:
'Even that Great Sage, my teacher, cannot know; how much less could his disciple know where I am?'"
Māra was immediately struck with fear, thinking:
"This śramaṇa has already perceived me!
He then transformed his entire body so that he emerged and stood before him.
Maudgalyāyana told Māra:
"In the distant past, during the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, I was once a Māra named Zhenhen (Hatred)."
"I have an elder sister named Āmra; at that time you were her son, and by this you may know that you are my sister's son.

At that time, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Krakucchanda Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. He had two disciples: one was called Mahāghoṣa and the other Vijñānagati; they were most honored, foremost, virtuous, and unsurpassed."
For what reason is the worthy one named Mahāghoṣa?
Dwelling in the Brahma-heaven, he utters a great sound that is heard throughout the trichiliocosm.
For what reason is the worthy one named Saṃjñājña?

If he dwells in seclusion, sitting beneath a tree, in a wilderness, or among the mountains, remaining in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) according to his physical form, those tending sheep or cattle, those carrying firewood or grass, and travelers passing through the fields will see him thus and say to one another:
"He has passed away here; let us each gather wood and carry grass to cremate him together with a funeral pyre."
Just as he had said, he immediately joined with the snake Vīra.

Then the bhikṣu Jñānasaṃjñin arose from his samādhi, shook out his robes to remove the dust and ashes, readjusted his dharma-robe, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city, towns, villages, and hamlets to wander for alms.
The cowherds and shepherds carrying firewood and grass were struck with amazement and said to one another:
"While we were dwelling in the wilderness, we saw this bhikṣu sitting beneath a tree without breathing; thinking he was dead, we gathered wood and grass together to cremate him."
"Now that perception is known, for this reason it is called 'perception-consciousness' (*saṃjñā-vijñāna*).
Thereupon, the Māra of Anger thought to himself:

'These śramaṇas claim to uphold the precepts; they practice silently and in stillness, contemplating as they go, just like a dog or a cat wishing to catch a mouse, remaining motionless until the mouse emerges, at which point they pounce. The śramaṇas’ meditative contemplation is exactly like this.'"

For example, when a heron wishes to catch fish, it remains silent and still, submerging its voice and contemplating the emergence of a fish so as to swallow it; the śramaṇas are also like this, silently contemplating and reflecting with single-minded focus on what they seek.

For example, it is like a great donkey that, having carried heavy burdens during the day, becomes utterly exhausted by night; starving and parched, it secretly longs for food and drink. The śramaṇas are just like this.
At that time, Māra thought to himself:

"I shall instead transform the elders and brahmins of this land, and seize those śramaṇas and practitioners who observe the precepts, beating them, reviling them, tearing their robes, breaking their bowls, and splitting their heads."
"I shall incite them to anger so that, by this means, I may find an opportunity.

Following this thought, he immediately transformed himself into the elders and brahmins of the kingdom; they seized the śramaṇas who observed the precepts and honored the Dharma, beating and reviling them, smashing their alms bowls, splitting open their heads, and tearing apart their robes.

These śramaṇas are like cats catching mice or cranes swallowing fish; they are like owls and crows catching mice among the trees. The śramaṇas practicing seated meditation are just like this, resembling donkeys exhausted by hunger.
At that time, all the bhikṣus, having been subjected to insults and humiliation, walked with downcast heads until they reached the abode of Krakucchanda Buddha.

While the Buddha was extensively expounding the Way and the sutras for the fourfold assembly of devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits, he saw the bhikṣus approaching, humiliated as they were, and addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus!"

Now, the Mara of Anger and Hatred transforms himself into elders and brahmins throughout various kingdoms, seizing those śramaṇas who uphold the precepts and honor the Dharma, beating them, reviling them, splitting their heads, breaking their bowls, and tearing their robes, causing their minds to become resentful and giving rise to thoughts of malice; by these means, he gains an opportunity to prevent them from achieving the Way.
In this regard, you should practice the four immeasurables:

loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Without harboring resentment or malice, and with a mind free from hatred, extend these qualities—vast, limitless, and universally peaceful—to the ten directions; though they may seek your vulnerability, they shall never find it.

The bhikṣu accepted the instruction and dwelt in seclusion in the wilderness, practicing single-minded dhyāna and contemplation; he cultivated the four immeasurables with a mind free from increase or decrease.
At that time, the Mara of Anger, though seeking an opportunity against the śramaṇa who upheld the precepts and honored the Dharma, was forever unable to find one.

"At that time, the brahmins and householders who had received the teachings of Māra reviled and insulted the śramaṇas who observed the precepts and upheld the Dharma; after their lives ended, they all returned to the evil realms—the places of diligent suffering, emaciation, affliction, and torture."

Within the hells, they receive their transformed bodies; they are like great trees, as vast as a great wilderness. Upon the ground of glowing iron, they cast themselves naked, each saying to themselves:

"We are of meager merit and our transgressions are violent and evil; we have seized and reviled śramaṇas who uphold the precepts and honor the Dharma. Here we take refuge and lament, yet we cannot see those śramaṇas who uphold the precepts and honor the Dharma. We sought an opportunity to encounter them, but having created this for ourselves, we now reap the calamity; we sit here following the teachings of Māra and fail to protect ourselves."
At that time, the Māra of Anger thought to himself:
"By this expedient means, I shall seek an opportunity against those śramaṇas who uphold the precepts, yet I can never find one;

I must certainly change my tactics and convert the householders and brahmins to provide robes, food, bedding, and medicine for the śramaṇas who uphold the precepts, causing them to crave such offerings, so that through these conditions I may gain an advantage."

Following this plan, he immediately transformed himself into an elder and a brahmin within the kingdom. Wherever there were roads with four-way intersections or narrow alleys, whenever he saw śramaṇas and practitioners upholding the precepts, he would spread his hair upon the ground and command them to walk over it, saying aloud:

"Śramaṇas who uphold the precepts cultivate their bodies and practice with diligence; they are difficult to encounter and difficult to meet. Pray, tread upon my hair so that I may obtain immeasurable merit throughout the long night."
Taking up his robes and carrying them, he went to that place, prostrated himself, and knelt for a long time, saying:
"I pray that you will take pity on me and accept these robes.
Carrying food in a basket or casket, he approached the vihāra, or offered it as a gift in the streets, lanes, and villages.
"A śramaṇa who upholds the precepts is difficult to encounter and difficult to meet; I pray that you will accept this offering so that I may obtain immeasurable merit throughout the long night.

He then embraced him, lifted him up, carried him as if on a shoulder, or transported him in a litter back to his house. Having seated him upon a fine couch, he brought forth various foods, drinks, clothing, *kāṣāya* robes, gold, silver, and the seven treasures, placing them before him.

Kneeling for a long time, he said: "A śramaṇa who upholds the precepts is difficult to encounter and difficult to see; I pray that you will accept this offering. Out of compassion for me, please let your desires be as you wish, so that I may obtain immeasurable merit throughout the long night."

"At that time, the Buddha Krukin, for the sake of the fourfold assembly, the devas, nāgas, and spirits, observed that the śramaṇas and practitioners who maintained the precepts were being honored, revered, and served in immeasurable ways by the elders and brahmins."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now, the Mara of Anger!

He has transformed various elders and brahmins, causing them to provide offerings of robes, food, bedding, and medicine to śramaṇas and practitioners who uphold the precepts. By allowing them to indulge their desires and become attached to such offerings, I shall take advantage of this circumstance to destroy their wholesome minds and prevent them from achieving the Way."

Because you dwell in seclusion among crags and in the wilderness, contemplating that all things are impermanent, even though you wear clothing and eat food, do not take pleasure in them through greed; they are suffering, empty, and not the self. Although Māra seeks an opportunity, he will ultimately be unable to find one.

The bhikṣus immediately accepted the teaching of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kruśānti; they practiced according to the Dharma, and although Māra sought an opportunity to harm them, he was never able to find one.
“The elders and brahmins who were converted by Māra were made to provide offerings to śramaṇas who uphold the precepts; through this merit, they were all reborn in the heavens.
Having been reborn in the heavens, each thought to himself:
‘We provided offerings to śramaṇas who uphold the Dharma and maintain pure precepts; we have obtained this blessing for ourselves, not from another, nor was it bestowed by the gods.’”
"At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda, after his meal and when the sun had declined, was traveling through various districts together with his great disciple Mahāghoṣa."

At that time, Māra the Evil One transformed himself into a great man, a valiant warrior, and stood by the side of the road holding a great club in his hand. He secretly raised the club and struck Hongyin on the head; the head was shattered and blood gushed forth, flowing profusely. At that moment, Pīṭhika remained behind the World-Honored One like a shadow following a form, silent and without a word.
At that time, the Tathāgata Krakucchanda, the Great Sage of Infinite Virtue, looked back with a sigh and spoke these words:
"Now, O Mara of Anger!
You do not know the limits of the great transgressions you have committed."

At that time, the Mara of Anger immediately fell into hell with this very body. He wallowed in hell like a fish or tadpole cast out onto dry land; it was as if his raw hide were being flayed, and he writhed upon the ground in unspeakable agony.

At that time, Māra Pāpīyas was wallowing in the hells in agonizing pain, many hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater than this; it was as if a person who had contracted a madness were running about, finding no place of rest.
"At that time, Māra Pāpīyān fell into the great hell and suffered immeasurable pain. Then, a being from the hells approached him and said:
'If you wish to know, my son, for every single tally-stick [that is counted], a bird flies into view; it is known that ten million years have passed, and even such instances are beyond limit.'"
"Evil Māra!
My lifespan in hell was such as this; only after that did I emerge from the great hell, yet I further encountered calamities for more than twenty-two thousand years."
At that time, the evil Māra was filled with great sorrow and distress.
The Buddha spoke these verses for Maudgalyāyana:
"What kind of hell is it Where the angry Māra must suffer his retribution?"
During the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, he transformed the assembly and his disciples;
whatever sufferings and afflictions they were to undergo, they all witnessed being subjected to punishment.
Fire blazed, burning their own bodies, its flames encircling their forms.
Such is that hell, the abode of the Mara of Anger.
During the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, the great disciple Mahāghoṣa,
even if he were before the Buddha and observing the assembly of bhikṣus, [would see it thus].
Because of conditions and causes one incurs transgression, and in an instant one becomes agitated.
If there is anyone who takes pleasure in criticizing others, that bhikṣu, a disciple of the Buddha,
will surely incur this calamity and head toward extreme suffering.
Like one who plunges into a deep abyss, abandoning the celestial palaces and no longer dwelling among the jade maidens, renouncing the pleasures of heaven—
those bhikṣus who are disciples of the Buddha are they who clearly understand this.
Since my awakening, I have emerged from [bondage], yet I am beset by harm and fallen into suffering.
O Māra, you should know that my body relies upon the gates of liberation;
I am not a celestial being dwelling among the gods, nor one renowned in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
If one discriminates in this way, a bhikṣu who is a disciple of the Buddha,
having committed unrighteousness himself, will thereby fall into an evil destiny.
Yet with but a single toe, he could cause the palace of the Most Victorious One to tremble.
Regarding the power of the divine feet (ṛddhipāda) by which Maudgalyāyana manifests great spiritual responses:
any bhikṣu who is a disciple of the Buddha and understands this clearly will establish themselves through their own efforts; how could they ever fall into the evil realms?
Even if there were a hundred beautiful women, exquisite and lovely jade-like maidens,
upon seeing a bhikṣu absorbed in dhyāna, they would not remain in the garden pavilion.
Even if one were to distinguish them thus, [they do not compare] to the bhikṣu, the disciple of the Buddha.
A bhikṣu fashions his own karma; he may even fall into the evil realms.
Even if he were to go together with all others to ask Śakra about this matter, would the Lord of Devas be able to explain it for him?
By what cause does one attain liberation?
Śākyamuni replied at that time: "One answers according to whatever is asked;
if one is oneself free from attachment, only then does one attain liberation."
If one understands this, a bhikṣu who is a disciple of the Buddha,
according to his own past actions, will himself arrive at and enter an evil destiny;
or he may reach the Brahma Heaven and pose difficult questions to the Brahmā King.
By what cause has one reached this place, And attained establishment in the Brahma-heaven?
The Brahma-king replied, answering his question:
"The place where I now stand Has never harbored false views."
Even from the Brahma Heaven, one may see the light recede;
what then shall I say now, as for whether my body shall endure forever?
If a bhikṣu, a disciple of the Buddha, understands this clearly, [he shall not fall].
When one personally commits unrighteous acts, one naturally returns to suffering.
That fire has no thoughts of its own, yet it shall burn away folly;
when the foolish and deluded themselves give rise to fire, they in turn endanger and burn their own bodies.
Pāpīyān, you should understand this: by directing your intent toward the Tathāgata, you bring peril upon yourself, like a fire burning a fool.
People delight in committing various evils for the sake of their own bodies throughout the long night.
Life comes without one’s own awareness; do not harass the bhikṣus.
O Māra, be careful not to test the Buddha, nor harass his disciples;
you shall find no peace for a long night, and you will surely fall into the evil realms.
At that time, Māra was subdued; because he feared the bhikṣu as he sat there, and having heard this, he became sorrowful and suddenly vanished on the spot.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all the devas, nāgas, and spirits were filled with joy.
The Scripture on Māra’s Temptation of Maudgalyāyana
